passage:
Vasudha stood in front of the small wooden mandir in the flat, matchbox in hand. The lamp had been lit every evening for years, but since Dada died last month the words had gone hollow in her mouth. She said them anyway and felt nothing, like knocking on a door with no house behind it.

Parul found her there. "You okay?"

"Why did God let it happen? He was kind to everyone. Or maybe nobody's listening. I don't know which is worse."

Parul didn't offer a neat answer, just sat down on the floor beside her. Vasudha didn't pretend to feel sure.

Later she asked Dadi, "Did you ever stop believing?" Dadi laughed softly. "After my own brother died, I didn't pray for a year. Ask me what I did instead." Vasudha nodded and struck the match.

qa.q: Who died last month?
qa.a: Dada died last month.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she said the prayer words?
qa.a: She felt empty and confused: the words had gone hollow in her mouth, and she said she did not know whether God let it happen or nobody is listening.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do next to stay honest about her doubt?
qa.a: She could keep asking elders like Dadi how they lived through doubt, read how others in her tradition have questioned, and stay truthful with Parul rather than forcing certainty. 🤍

qa.q: How might Parul feel sitting on the floor beside Vasudha?
qa.a: Parul probably feels unsure what to say but chooses to stay close instead of offering a neat answer, which makes it safe for Vasudha to be honest.

grounding: After a loss Vasudha asks why God let it happen and prayer feels empty, while she stays honest and turns to an elder.

passage:
Come, sit, Chinmay. You've been very quiet lately, so let me tell you about the year I turned twenty. I'm Thomas, and I don't tell this often.

That year a flood took the house and the shop in one night. We had done nothing wrong, and I was furious. For a month I said nothing to anyone. I went to church, I sang, I felt like a wall.

Then one night I stood alone in the empty pews and shouted at God. Every ugly thing I could think of.

Old Mrs. Pillai found me there. She didn't scold. She put the book of Psalms in my hands. "Half of it is people complaining to God," she said.

Neighbours brought rice and blankets for weeks. The anger didn't vanish, but it stopped turning to stone.

qa.q: What took the house and the shop in one night?
qa.a: A flood took the house and the shop in one night.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel in the first month, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Thomas was furious and shut down: no words to anyone and feeling like a wall, until the anger came out as shouting in the empty pews.

qa.q: What helped Thomas, and what could Chinmay take from it?
qa.a: Letting the anger be spoken, the Psalms and the neighbours' rice and blankets helped, so Chinmay could let anger speak and lean on people nearby instead of swallowing it.

qa.q: How does Mrs. Pillai see Thomas's shouting?
qa.a: Mrs. Pillai does not scold; by handing over the Psalms and saying half of it is complaining, she treats the protest as something faith can hold.

grounding: Thomas is angry at God for undeserved suffering, lets the anger speak, and is held by time, text and neighbours.

passage:
Chetan, your parents told me you've been asking questions about the puja, and that they're frightened. Sit. I'm Saurabh, and I was twenty once.

I stopped joining the evening aarti and one day said, "Why waste an hour on this?" My mother's face fell. My father went silent. Later I heard her tell a neighbour, "We've lost him."

That hurt. That night I sat with her and said, "Amma, I love you. I'm not leaving anything. I just have questions." I still ate the prasad she handed me. A week later I asked my father, gently, what the aarti gave him.

He said, "It's how my mother sat with me." We never agreed on everything. But after that, nobody in the house was afraid.

qa.q: What did Saurabh's mother say to a neighbour?
qa.a: She said, "We've lost him."

qa.q: What were Saurabh's parents feeling when he stopped joining the aarti?
qa.a: They were afraid: his mother's face fell and she told a neighbour they had lost him, while his father went silent.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that eased the fear, and what else could Chetan try?
qa.a: Saurabh told his mother he loved her and only had questions, ate the prasad, and asked his father gently what the aarti gave him; Chetan could share questions the same gentle way. 🙂

qa.q: What might the aarti mean to Saurabh's father?
qa.a: It seems to be a memory and a closeness, since he said it is how his mother sat with him, not a challenge to Saurabh.

grounding: Saurabh's parents fear his questions mean he is losing his way, and he reassures them, shares gently and avoids mocking their rituals.

passage:
I'm Kunal, and the strangest part wasn't the questions, it was the silence after. I'd asked the temple committee why we do one ritual the way we do, and whether it had to be this way. Not to be rude. I wanted to know.

The next Sunday, aunties who used to press prasad into my hand looked past me. Talk stopped when I walked up. I stood by the shoe rack feeling like a stranger in a place I grew up in. Honestly, I was angry. I almost decided never to go back.

What changed things was Samir Uncle, who kept the temple library. He said, "Come, help me sort these books. Questions are fine here." And one friend from the youth group kept sitting next to me.

I don't agree with everyone there. But those two mattered more than any argument.

qa.q: Who kept the temple library?
qa.a: Samir Uncle kept the temple library.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel standing by the shoe rack?
qa.a: Kunal felt like a stranger in a place Kunal grew up in, lonely and angry enough to nearly decide never to go back.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Kunal to hold on to a couple of people?
qa.a: Samir Uncle and the friend welcomed questions, so Kunal did not have to cut every tie in anger and could keep the community through people, not doctrine.

qa.q: How might the aunties see Kunal's questions?
qa.a: The aunties may hear the questions as a challenge to something they love, so they go quiet, which could be discomfort rather than a plan to shun Kunal.

grounding: People in the temple go cold when Kunal questions, Kunal feels lonely, and finds one elder and one peer who stay open.

passage:
I'm Sunaina. Relief came first, Vikas. I remember sitting on my hostel bed after saying to myself, for the first time, that I don't believe in God. My chest felt lighter, like putting down a bag I'd carried since childhood.

Then the loneliness arrived. At Diwali I stood in the kitchen while my mother and aunts sang, and I didn't know where I fit.

For a while I was a little proud of being the rational one. I rolled my eyes at things. Then my grandmother caught me at it and asked quietly, "Does it hurt you if I pray?" It didn't. That stopped me.

Now I try to say what I actually live by: telling the truth, showing up for people. I go to the puja for my family and sit through it respectfully.

qa.q: Where was Sunaina sitting when the relief came?
qa.a: Sunaina was sitting on the hostel bed.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel after the relief, and what shows it?
qa.a: Loneliness: at Diwali Sunaina stood in the kitchen while the others sang and didn't know where to fit.

qa.q: What did the grandmother's question help change?
qa.a: It stopped the eye-rolling pride, and now Sunaina names values like telling the truth and showing up for people while respecting believers by sitting through the puja.

qa.q: How might the grandmother feel about the eye-rolling?
qa.a: The grandmother may feel a little hurt or curious, but asks quietly rather than scolding, which suggests she wants to understand.

grounding: Sunaina settles into being an atheist, feels relief and some loneliness, and chooses named values and respect for believers over pride.

passage:
Before dawn, Irfan unrolled his prayer mat in the corner of the room, careful not to wake his brothers. In the city hostel last year, someone had asked how he could believe anything, and he'd had no good answer. He still didn't. Some mornings he wasn't sure anyone was listening.

But standing there, hands folded, the noise in his head slowed down. The cool floor, the words he'd known since childhood, the first rooster outside. His breathing evened out.

At the well, his neighbour Pooja asked, "Aren't you doubtful these days?"

"Yes," he said. "It still steadies me. I don't need every answer to do it."

Then he added, "But I'll ask the teacher my questions. I don't want to hide behind this."

qa.q: What did Irfan unroll before dawn?
qa.a: Irfan unrolled his prayer mat before dawn.

qa.q: Why does Irfan keep praying even though he is unsure?
qa.a: It steadies him: the noise in his head slows down and his breathing evens out, even on mornings when he isn't sure anyone is listening.

qa.q: Why is asking the teacher a sensible addition to Irfan's prayer?
qa.a: It keeps the practice from becoming a way to avoid his real questions, so he can pray and still ask honestly.

qa.q: What might Pooja be thinking when asking about the doubts?
qa.a: Pooja may be curious or concerned and has noticed something different in Irfan, asking plainly at the well rather than judging.

grounding: Irfan keeps praying despite doubt because it steadies him, and he also plans to ask his questions instead of hiding behind ritual.

passage:
Nadia was folding laundry in her Melbourne share house when her phone lit up. Xin had posted a joke comparing people who pray to people waiting for a bus that never comes. Forty likes already, and comments laughing at "believers".

Her face went hot. It wasn't about the bus. It felt like her grandmother's prayer beads and her own quiet mornings had just been called silly in front of everyone. She typed a reply sneering at Xin's "empty" life, and stopped.

She deleted it. Then she scrolled to something Xin had sent last week: "Honest question, what does praying actually feel like for you?"

She answered that one, warmly and at length. The joke she left alone, unliked and unanswered.

qa.q: In which city was Nadia folding laundry?
qa.a: Nadia was in her Melbourne share house.

qa.q: Why did Nadia's face go hot?
qa.a: It felt like her grandmother's prayer beads and her own quiet mornings had been called silly in front of everyone.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the sneering reply and answering Xin's honest question worked, because it avoided matching contempt with contempt while still engaging real curiosity.

qa.q: How might Xin see the joke and the honest question?
qa.a: Xin may see the joke as ordinary humour among friends, while the honest question shows real interest in Nadia's life, and may not realise the joke hurt.

grounding: A friend mocks belief online and Nadia feels attacked, but she separates the ridicule from the honest question and answers only the question.

passage:
Shalini, sit. I'm Lalremsiami, and I'll tell you about my friend Zoliana and a day I nearly said something unkind.

I was twenty and my doubts were heavy. Zoliana, who sang in the church choir, patted my shoulder and said, "Just have faith." Irritation rose in me like heat. It sounded like what people say when they don't want to hear the hard part. I almost said, "That's a stupid thing to believe."

I bit my tongue and asked, "What does faith give you, Zoliana?"

He was quiet, then said, "When my father was away, it felt like I wasn't alone." I hadn't known that.

So I said, "I need someone to listen to my questions, not fix them." He nodded. Since then he asks first.

qa.q: What did Zoliana say that irritated Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Zoliana said, "Just have faith."

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when Zoliana said it?
qa.a: Irritation, like heat rising, and a wish to be heard on the hard part; Lalremsiami almost called the belief stupid but held back.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that kept the friendship?
qa.a: Lalremsiami asked what faith gives Zoliana and then said what was needed, someone to listen, instead of calling the belief stupid.

qa.q: What was it like for Zoliana to be asked what faith gives him?
qa.a: Zoliana went quiet and then shared that faith made him feel less alone while his father was away, so the question let him speak personally instead of feeling judged.

grounding: Lalremsiami is irritated by a devout friend's 'just have faith', asks what faith gives him and shares what is needed.

passage:
Dear Uday,

I went with Mausi to the satsang on Sunday, and I haven't stopped thinking about it. Hundreds of people sat in rows. When the guru walked in, everyone bowed until their foreheads touched the floor. Nobody looked up until he had passed.

A boy near me asked a small question about a teaching. The guru smiled, but the people around us hushed the boy and said, "Guruji is beyond questions." The boy went red.

A bag for donations also went round, and a lady told me that giving more brings blessings faster.

I did feel something in that hall, a stillness. But I'm not sure I'd want a teacher nobody can question. Tell me what you think.

Pallavi

qa.q: Who did Pallavi go to the satsang with?
qa.a: Pallavi went with Mausi.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Pallavi describe about the satsang?
qa.a: Pallavi felt a stillness in the hall but is not sure about wanting a teacher nobody can question.

qa.q: What signs would show that a teacher is genuine?
qa.a: A genuine teacher welcomes questions, has accountability, and does not take money or obedience beyond reason, unlike the hushing and the donation pressure Pallavi saw.

qa.q: How did the boy who asked the question likely feel?
qa.a: The boy probably felt embarrassed, since he went red when the people around hushed him for asking.

grounding: A guru surrounded by devotees is treated as beyond question, and Pallavi, watching its effect on others, doubts a teacher no one may question.

passage:
Sharmila: Didi, can I tell you something without you getting angry?
Minakshi: Of course. What's wrong?
Sharmila: At the retreat group, I asked why nobody checks how the donations are used. They said my doubt is just ego.
Minakshi: Who said that?
Sharmila: The senior members. And the teacher says if I leave, bad luck will follow our family. I lie awake now. Maybe I'm being selfish.
Minakshi: You're shaking. When did you stop sleeping?
Sharmila: Since Tuesday. I feel guilty even asking.
Minakshi: Sharmi, a group that makes you afraid and guilty for asking questions is waving a red flag. That's not on you.
Sharmila: But what if something bad happens?
Minakshi: Let's sit with Mummy and Papa tonight, and call your college friends too. No deciding alone, okay?
Sharmila: Okay. Thank you for not shouting.

qa.q: Since which day has Sharmila been unable to sleep?
qa.a: Sharmila has not slept since Tuesday.

qa.q: What is Sharmila afraid of, and how does the guilt show?
qa.a: Sharmila fears bad luck will follow the family if Sharmila leaves, lies awake, and asks whether questioning is selfish, feeling guilty even asking.

qa.q: What would you advise Sharmila to do before deciding?
qa.a: Talk with Mummy, Papa and friends outside the group, remembering that fear and guilt used for control are red flags, and not decide alone. 🤍

qa.q: How does Minakshi see the group's answer to Sharmila's question?
qa.a: Minakshi sees it as a red flag about the group, not a fault in Sharmila, because a group that makes someone afraid and guilty for asking is the worrying party.

grounding: Sharmila is told doubting the teacher is ego and that leaving brings misfortune, and Minakshi names fear and guilt as red flags and urges talking outside the group.
